name: Eliminative Materialism
statement: Our everyday talk of beliefs and desires may be a false theory that neuroscience will discard, not confirm.
statementAccent: a false theory that neuroscience will discard
meaning: Eliminative materialism, or eliminativism, is a radical physicalist view in the philosophy of mind, holding that our ordinary, common-sense understanding of the mind, called folk psychology, is a deeply mistaken theory, and that some or all of the mental states it posits, such as beliefs and desires, do not actually exist. On this view, folk psychology, which explains and predicts behavior in terms of beliefs, desires, intentions, and the like, is an implicit theory that could turn out to be false, just as many past theories have been. Eliminativists argue that as neuroscience matures, folk-psychological concepts will not be reduced to or vindicated by brain science but will instead be eliminated and replaced by a more accurate neuroscientific account, much as the concept of phlogiston was eliminated rather than reduced when chemistry advanced. The leading contemporary defenders are Paul Churchland and Patricia Churchland, with earlier figures including Wilfrid Sellars, Paul Feyerabend, and Richard Rorty. Eliminative materialism contrasts sharply with reductive physicalism, which holds that mental states are real and identical to brain states; the eliminativist denies that the states of folk psychology are real at all. The view is provocative and widely regarded as extreme, and it faces the notable objection that asserting it seems to presuppose the very beliefs it denies.
mechanism: Eliminative materialism treats folk psychology as an empirical theory and then argues that the theory is false. Common-sense psychology, on this account, is a network of generalizations that explain and predict behavior by attributing internal states such as beliefs and desires, for example the generalization that if someone desires something and believes a certain action will get it, they will tend to perform that action. Because folk psychology is a theory, eliminativists argue, its central posits, beliefs and desires, could fail to correspond to anything real, just as the posits of earlier discarded theories did. Their argument for elimination rather than reduction has several strands. They contend that folk psychology has been stagnant, failing to progress for millennia, and that it fails to explain a wide range of phenomena, such as mental illness, sleep, memory, learning, and consciousness. They point to the poor fit between the sentence-like, propositional structure that folk psychology attributes to beliefs and the very different architecture of the brain, with its neurons, firing rates, and spreading activation. And they draw an inductive lesson from the history of science, in which many folk theories proved radically mistaken and their entities eliminated, like phlogiston, caloric, vital spirits, witches, and the four humors. The conclusion is that a mature neuroscience will replace folk psychology, so that beliefs and desires will be eliminated rather than identified with brain states.

examples.text: Eliminativists treat common-sense psychology, which explains behavior by beliefs and desires, as an implicit theory that could be false.
Just as chemistry eliminated phlogiston rather than reducing it, neuroscience may eliminate beliefs and desires.
Unlike reductive physicalism, which identifies mental states with brain states, eliminativism denies they exist at all.

variants.name: The Churchlands' neurophilosophy
variants.text: The leading contemporary defense, arguing that a mature neuroscience will replace folk psychology rather than vindicate it.

variants.name: The self-refutation objection
variants.text: The charge that asserting eliminativism presupposes having beliefs, so denying beliefs exist is self-undermining.

whyItMatters: Eliminative materialism is a provocative and important position in the philosophy of mind, staking out the most radical form of physicalism and forcing the field to confront how much of our common-sense picture of the mind might be mistaken. By arguing that folk psychology is a theory that could be false, and that beliefs and desires might go the way of phlogiston, eliminativism challenges the deep assumption that the mental states we take for granted are real, and it dramatizes the possibility that a mature neuroscience could overturn our self-understanding rather than confirm it. This makes eliminativism a valuable foil in debates about the mind, sharpening the contrast with reductive physicalism, which preserves mental states by identifying them with brain states, and with non-reductive and dualist views that treat the mental as robustly real. The position raises fundamental questions about the status of folk psychology, the relationship between common sense and science, and what it would mean for a scientific revolution to reach the mind itself. Even critics, who find the view deeply counterintuitive and press the self-refutation objection, engage it seriously.

limits: Eliminative materialism is deeply counterintuitive and faces a powerful objection. The self-refutation, or self-defeating, objection holds that the very act of asserting eliminative materialism seems to presuppose that the eliminativist believes the theory is true, so denying that beliefs exist appears to undermine itself. Eliminativists reply that this objection begs the question by assuming the folk-psychological account of assertion and belief that eliminativism disputes, and that folk vocabulary can be used provisionally, as one might still speak of phlogiston while rejecting it, until a neuroscientific replacement matures; whether this reply succeeds is debated. The view is also speculative, resting on a prediction about the future course of neuroscience that has not been borne out, and many hold that some form of folk psychology will be preserved or vindicated rather than eliminated.
misreadings: Eliminative materialism is not the reductive claim that beliefs and desires are brain states; it is the stronger claim that they do not exist at all and will be eliminated, not identified. It is a prediction about a mature neuroscience, not an established result, and remains speculative. And the self-refutation objection, that asserting it presupposes belief, is a serious challenge rather than a knockdown, since eliminativists dispute its assumptions, so treating eliminativism as reductive physicalism, as proven, or as obviously self-refuting without reply, misreads a radical and contested view.
origin: A radical physicalist view in philosophy of mind, defended notably by Paul and Patricia Churchland with roots in Sellars, Feyerabend, and Rorty, holding that folk psychology is a false theory whose posits like beliefs will be eliminated by neuroscience.

sources.text: Eliminative Materialism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — folk psychology as a theory that may be false, the claim that beliefs and desires do not exist, the phlogiston analogy, the Churchlands and earlier figures, the arguments for elimination, and the self-refutation objection and reply.
Paul Churchland, Eliminative Materialism and the Propositional Attitudes (1981). — the foundational modern statement of eliminative materialism and its case against folk psychology.
